steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on making a human-sized bipedal robot run using a CPG-based controller with fast and slow adaptations of actuation timing. Cover the background on passive dynamics and simple walking/running models, CPG-based control inspired by neurophysiology, the gap in adjusting muscle firing timing, and what we propose and how we validate it.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Our passive-dynamics-based bipedal robots; simple walking and running models
- Neurophysiology-based control: central pattern generators (CPGs)
- Gait emerging from CPG interaction; phase resetting; CPG + machine learning
- Gap: muscle firing timing relative to gait cycle; slow adaptation
- Our proposal: CPG controller with fast and slow adaptations, validation

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Passive dynamics
  - we develop human-sized bipedal robots based on passive dynamic mechanisms (important in human locomotion)
  - McGeer: simple robot, passive legs at hip, walks stably down a slope with only gravity (cite)
  - -> passive locomotion important in gait; but mechanisms hard to understand from observation alone
  - simple walking models (cite)
  - running too: SLIP model, point mass + prismatic massless spring, reproduces running dynamics (cite)
  - our earlier robot using bouncing rod dynamics (cite); recent robot with actuators imitating human musculoskeletal system, using passive dynamics (cite)
- Neurophysiology
  - walking/running = interaction of nervous system, body, environment -> controllers based on human neurophysiology
  - patterned locomotion centers at lower levels of CNS (spinal cord, brainstem), simulated via CPGs (cite)
  - CPGs: hierarchical network, rhythm generators + pattern formulators (timing of muscle activation)
  - Rybak et al.: model of mammalian spinal cord circuits, firing patterns of muscle activity; CPGs from cats with spinal cord disconnected from higher centers; can temporarily reset muscle activity on sensory input (cite)
- CPG interaction
  - gait emerges from interaction of CPGs assigned to legs, dynamical models and legged robots (cite)
  - Aoi and Tsuchiya: stable walking in bipedal compass model, adaptive gait period, CPG with phase resetting inspired by rhythm resetting in human walking (cite)
  - ML + CPG controller -> optimal relation between CPG phase and motor control (cite)
- Gap
  - humans fire muscles at same rate relative to gait cycle in running (cite) -> robots should reproduce this
  - CPG with phase resetting only: period adapts, but muscle firing timing cannot be adjusted
  - Fujiki et al.: slow (late) adaptation from neurophysiological findings (cite) + phase resetting, compact biped on split-belt with different left/right velocities -> converges to steady-state gait (cite)
- Proposal
  - adaptive control system based on human neurophysiology, stable running in human-sized biped
  - unlike ML studies optimizing controllers, CPG-based design to reveal how robot + controller manage environment by adaptive behavior
  - adjust actuation timings via fast and slow adaptations
  - rhythm generator: phase angular velocity adjusted via fast adaptation (phase resetting) and slow adaptation to actual gait cycle
  - pattern formulator: muscle activation timing from leg-state feedback -> running pattern
  - validation: numerical simulations of simple running model + experiments on bipedal robot

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
We have been developing human-sized bipedal robots that are based on passive dynamic mechanisms, because these play a significant role in human dynamical locomotion. McGeer developed a simple bipedal robot that had passive legs attached to the hip, and this robot could walk stably by descending a slope without any energy input except gravity. This study showed that passive locomotion can play a significant role in gait. However, the dynamical mechanisms of this kind of locomotion are complex and hard to fully understand only from observation. So to overcome the limits of the observational approach, several researchers investigated gait mechanisms with simple walking models. But bipedal locomotion is not only walking, it is also running. So some researchers further developed simple running models. For example, the spring-loaded inverted pendulum (SLIP) model, which is made of a point mass and a prismatic massless spring, can reproduce the dynamics of running effectively. Until now, to realize the running motion, we developed a bipedal robot that uses bouncing rod dynamics. Recently we developed a bipedal robot with actuators that can imitate the human musculoskeletal system, while still using the passive nature of the dynamics of the robot.

Walking and running are executed through dynamic interactions between the nervous system, the body, and the environment. So bipedal robot controllers have been proposed that are based on human neurophysiology. It is reported that the centers that execute patterned locomotion in humans, like walking and running, exist at the lower levels of the central nervous system (e.g., the spinal cord and brainstem), and these are simulated with central pattern generators (CPGs). CPGs use a hierarchical network of rhythm generators, which generate the rhythm of walking and running, and pattern formulators, which are responsible for the timing of muscle activation. Rybak et al. developed a model of mammalian spinal cord circuits and investigated the firing patterns of muscle activity. They included CPGs obtained by observing muscle activity in cats whose spinal cord was disconnected from the higher centers, and the model can temporarily reset muscle activity when there is sensory input from the limbs.

- gait emerges from interaction of CPGs assigned to legs, dynamical models and legged robots
- Aoi and Tsuchiya: stable walking in bipedal compass model, adaptive gait period, CPG with phase resetting (inspired by rhythm resetting in human walking)
- ML + CPG controller -> optimal relation between CPG phase and motor control
- Gap
  - humans fire muscles at same rate relative to gait cycle in running -> robots should reproduce
  - phase resetting only: period adapts, muscle firing timing not adjustable
  - Fujiki et al.: slow (late) adaptation from neurophysiological findings + phase resetting, compact biped on split-belt, different left/right velocities -> steady-state gait
- Proposal
  - adaptive control based on human neurophysiology, stable running, human-sized biped
  - not ML optimization; CPG-based, reveal how robot + controller manage environment by adaptive behavior
  - rhythm generator: phase angular velocity via fast adaptation (phase resetting) + slow adaptation to actual gait cycle
  - pattern formulator: muscle activation timing from leg-state feedback
  - validation: simulations of simple running model, experiments on bipedal robot

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
We have been developing human-sized bipedal robots that are based on passive dynamic mechanisms, because these play a significant role in human dynamical locomotion. McGeer developed a simple bipedal robot that had passive legs attached to the hip, and this robot could walk stably by descending a slope without any energy input except gravity. This study showed that passive locomotion can play a significant role in gait. However, the dynamical mechanisms of this kind of locomotion are complex and hard to fully understand only from observation. So to overcome the limits of the observational approach, several researchers investigated gait mechanisms with simple walking models. But bipedal locomotion is not only walking, it is also running. So some researchers further developed simple running models. For example, the spring-loaded inverted pendulum (SLIP) model, which is made of a point mass and a prismatic massless spring, can reproduce the dynamics of running effectively. Until now, to realize the running motion, we developed a bipedal robot that uses bouncing rod dynamics. Recently we developed a bipedal robot with actuators that can imitate the human musculoskeletal system, while still using the passive nature of the dynamics of the robot.

Walking and running are executed through dynamic interactions between the nervous system, the body, and the environment. So bipedal robot controllers have been proposed that are based on human neurophysiology. It is reported that the centers that execute patterned locomotion in humans, like walking and running, exist at the lower levels of the central nervous system (e.g., the spinal cord and brainstem), and these are simulated with central pattern generators (CPGs). CPGs use a hierarchical network of rhythm generators, which generate the rhythm of walking and running, and pattern formulators, which are responsible for the timing of muscle activation. Rybak et al. developed a model of mammalian spinal cord circuits and investigated the firing patterns of muscle activity. They included CPGs obtained by observing muscle activity in cats whose spinal cord was disconnected from the higher centers, and the model can temporarily reset muscle activity when there is sensory input from the limbs.

Several researchers investigated how gait emerges through the interaction of CPGs that are assigned to legs, using dynamical models and legged robots. Aoi and Tsuchiya reported that stable walking can be achieved in a bipedal compass model by changing the gait period adaptively with a CPG that involves phase resetting, which is inspired by the rhythm resetting in human walking. Recently some researchers combined machine learning and a CPG controller to find the optimal relationship between the CPG phase and the motor control.

It can be observed that humans fire their muscles at the same rate relative to the gait cycle when running. So to achieve adaptive running with robots, this characteristic should be reproduced. If a CPG is used only with phase resetting for running control, the overall period can be varied adaptively, but it is not yet possible to adjust the timing of muscle firing. Also, Fujiki et al. reported that when slow adaptation (late adaptation) is applied to the CPG based on the neurophysiological findings in addition to phase resetting, to control a compact bipedal robot walking on a split-belt with different velocities of the left and right limbs, the motion converges to a steady-state gait.

In this study we propose an adaptive control system based on the current knowledge of human neurophysiology, to achieve a stable running condition in a human-sized bipedal robot. Machine learning studies explore optimized controllers for the environment, but here we designed the controller based on CPG, with the aim to reveal how the robot and controller manage to the environment by adaptive behavior. Our aim was to achieve adaptive running of the bipedal robot by adjusting the actuation timings with fast and slow adaptations. We designed a CPG-based controller that shows adaptive behavior by providing fast and slow adaptations. Specifically, in the rhythm generator the phase angular velocity is adjusted with fast adaptation (phase resetting) and slow adaptation to the actual gait cycle. Also, the pattern formulator adjusts the muscle activation timing based on the leg-state feedback to produce a running pattern. We validated the proposed control system with numerical simulations of a simple running model and with experiments on a bipedal robot.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
We have been developing human-sized bipedal robots based on passive dynamic mechanisms, which play a significant role in human dynamical locomotion. McGeer [1] developed a simple bipedal robot with passive legs attached to the hip; this robot could walk stably by descending a slope, without any energy input other than gravity. This study indicated that passive locomotion can play a significant role in gait. However, the dynamical mechanisms of such locomotion are complex and hard to fully understand from observation alone. To overcome the limitations of the observational approach, several researchers have investigated gait mechanisms using simple walking models [2,3,4,5,6,7,8]. Bipedal locomotion consists not only of walking but also of running, and therefore some researchers further developed simple running models. For example, the spring-loaded inverted pendulum (SLIP) model, comprising a point mass and a prismatic massless spring, can effectively reproduce the dynamics of running [9,10,11,12,13,14]. To realize the running motion, we previously developed a bipedal robot that utilizes bouncing rod dynamics [15]. Recently, we developed a bipedal robot with actuators that imitate the human musculoskeletal system while utilizing the passive nature of the robot's dynamics [16].

Walking and running are executed through dynamic interactions between the nervous system, body, and environment. Accordingly, bipedal robot controllers have been proposed based on human neurophysiology. The centers involved in executing patterned locomotion in humans, such as walking and running, are reported to exist at the lower levels of the central nervous system (e.g., the spinal cord and brainstem), and they are simulated via central pattern generators (CPGs) [17,18,19,20,21,22]. CPGs employ a hierarchical network of rhythm generators, which generate the rhythm of walking and running, and pattern formulators, which are responsible for the timing of muscle activation. Rybak et al. [17] developed a model of mammalian spinal cord circuits and investigated the firing patterns of muscle activity. They incorporated CPGs obtained by observing muscle activity in cats whose spinal cord was disconnected from the higher centers, and their model can temporarily reset muscle activity upon sensory input from the limbs.

Several researchers have investigated the emergence of gait through the interaction of CPGs assigned to the legs, using dynamical models and legged robots [23,24,25,26,27,28,29]. Aoi and Tsuchiya [30,31] reported that stable walking can be achieved in a bipedal compass model by adaptively changing the gait period using a CPG with phase resetting, inspired by the rhythm resetting of human walking. Recently, some researchers have combined machine learning and CPG controllers to reveal the optimal relationship between CPG phase and motor control [32,33,34,35].

Humans can be observed to fire their muscles at the same rate relative to the gait cycle during running [36]. Thus, such a characteristic should be reproduced to achieve adaptive running with robots. When a CPG is used solely with phase resetting for running control, the overall period can be adaptively varied, but adjusting the timing of muscle firing is not yet achievable. Moreover, Fujiki et al. [37] reported that when slow adaptation (late adaptation) based on neurophysiological findings [38] is applied to a CPG in addition to phase resetting to control a compact bipedal robot walking on a split-belt with different velocities for the left and right limbs, the motion converges to a steady-state gait.

This study proposes an adaptive control system, based on current knowledge of human neurophysiology, to achieve stable running in a human-sized bipedal robot. Unlike machine learning studies that explore optimized controllers for the environment, we designed a CPG-based controller with the aim of revealing how the robot and controller manage to the environment through adaptive behavior. We aimed to achieve adaptive running of the bipedal robot by adjusting the actuation timings via fast and slow adaptations, and designed the CPG-based controller to manifest adaptive behavior through these two adaptations. Specifically, in the rhythm generator, the phase angular velocity is adjusted via fast adaptation (phase resetting) and slow adaptation to the actual gait cycle. The pattern formulator then adjusts the muscle activation timing on the basis of leg-state feedback to yield a running pattern. We validated the proposed control system through numerical simulations of a simple running model and through experiments on a bipedal robot.
